raw_response:
I'm 42 and I've been farming these 5 mu since I was 17. My old man passed down what he knew, and I've learned the rest by doing — good years, bad years, droughts, price crashes. Five mu isn't enough to live on by itself, so my wife works at a garment factory in town and my daughter just started working off-farm too. That money helps with the household, but it also means I'm mostly alone in the fields with my father, who's getting old and can't do heavy work anymore.

The maize is nearly ready to harvest — I'll get it off in the next week. Then I need to turn around and get the wheat in the ground by mid-October. There's no rest on a small farm.

For the **winter wheat**, I'll plant around October 12th. I always use an improved Jinmai variety — I'll buy fresh certified seed this year, about 14 kg per mu at roughly 5 yuan per kg. The extension agent says certified seed germinates better, and I've seen the difference myself. Before planting, I'll run the rotary tiller over the field to break up the maize stubble. Then I put down base fertilizer: about 50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer, the 15-15-15 type. That's what I've used for years and I know it works. In late March, when the wheat starts jointing, I'll topdress with 15 kg per mu of urea. Last year my neighbor Wang tried to save 30 yuan per mu by cutting his urea rate, and his wheat turned yellow at heading — he lost maybe 60 kg per mu. I'm not making that mistake. The extension says 15 kg nitrogen per mu is about right, but with my soil I figure I need the full 14–15 kg total. Better to waste a little fertilizer than to lose yield.

I irrigate wheat three times: once before winter to protect against freeze, once at jointing in March, and once during grain filling in May. Each time costs about 25 yuan per mu for the electricity to pump, but without it the yield drops by more than that. Water is expensive but necessary — last spring was dry and the farmers who skipped the jointing irrigation really suffered. I'll spray herbicide in early spring, and if I see aphids in April I'll spray insecticide too. All the field work is me and my father. For 5 mu we don't hire labor — can't afford it. The only thing I hire is the combine for harvest in early June. I expect about 420 kg per mu if the weather holds. Last year I got 418 kg, so that's realistic.

For **summer maize**, the window is brutal — wheat comes off around June 10th, and I need to get maize in the ground by June 15th or I lose too much growing time. No time for deep tillage. I plant Zhengdan 958 hybrid, about 2.5 kg per mu. Direct seeding into the wheat stubble with minimal tillage — that's the only way to make the timing work on 5 mu. At planting I put down 40 kg per mu of compound fertilizer, then when the plants are knee-high around mid-July, I topdress with 10 kg of urea. That's about 12 kg of nitrogen per mu total. Some of the bigger farms do 18–20 kg, but with maize prices what they are, I can't afford to throw money at the crop. I need to cover my costs, not set records.

Maize gets two irrigations: one before tasseling in late July, and one during grain filling in August. If the summer rains are good I might skip the second one, but I plan for two. Herbicide at planting, and I watch for corn borers — if I see damage, I'll spray. Harvest is late September or early October, again with a hired combine. I expect about 460 kg per mu. Last year I got 455 kg, so I'm being a little cautious.

The total input cost for both crops runs me about 3,650 yuan for the 5 mu. That's a lot of money for a smallholder like me, but I've learned that under-investing costs more in the end. Still, every yuan I spend on fertilizer is a yuan I don't have for my daughter's school expenses, so I watch it closely. I don't optimize — I do what works, what I can afford, and what keeps my family fed.
